purpose: Assesses whether the organization can detect or prevent an adversary removing stolen data from the environment.
summary: Exfiltration consists of techniques adversaries use to steal data out of the network, such as transferring it over the command-and-control channel, over an alternate protocol, over physical media, or through automated exfiltration of large data sets to external destinations.
expectedStatementElements: What data loss prevention (DLP) controls monitor and block unauthorized outbound transfer of sensitive data
How the organization detects unusually large or unusually timed outbound data transfers
What controls limit exfiltration over alternate channels (removable media, personal cloud storage, unauthorized protocols)
How exfiltration attempts are correlated with earlier-stage indicators (collection, staging) to catch an attack before data leaves
evidenceExamples: DLP tool configuration and policy covering sensitive data types and channels
Network monitoring/alerting configuration for anomalous outbound transfer volume or timing
Removable media and unsanctioned cloud storage restriction policy and enforcement
Correlation rules linking exfiltration-stage alerts with earlier collection/staging indicators
commonGaps: DLP coverage is incomplete, missing key sensitive data types or channels like personal email or cloud storage
Unusually large or oddly timed outbound transfers aren't flagged for review
Removable media or unsanctioned cloud storage services aren't restricted or monitored
Exfiltration alerts are treated in isolation rather than correlated with earlier signs of collection or staging
interviewQuestions: Does your DLP actually cover the data types and channels that matter most, or are there known gaps?
Would an unusually large or oddly timed outbound transfer get flagged for review?
Are removable media and personal cloud storage services restricted or monitored?
If exfiltration were detected, would it be connected to earlier warning signs, or treated as a standalone event?
